Title: Ishtar Gate
Description: The glazed-brick gate of Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon was excavated by a German team under Robert Koldewey. Its fragments were packed into barrels and shipped to Berlin, where the front gate was rebuilt inside the museum. Iraq has repeatedly asked Germany to return it, notably in 2002 and 2009.
Story: Babylon, on the Euphrates south of today's Baghdad, was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Around 575 BCE King Nebuchadnezzar II built the Ishtar Gate as the eighth gate of the inner city and dedicated it to Ishtar, goddess of love and war. Its blue glazed bricks imitated lapis lazuli and carried rows of dragons, bulls and lions, the animals of the gods Marduk, Adad and Ishtar. Every New Year, statues of the gods were carried through the gate along the Processional Way. For the people of Babylon it was the ceremonial entrance to their city; for modern Iraq it has become a national symbol, echoed in the facades of Iraqi embassies abroad.

Title: Pergamon Altar
Description: Carl Humann excavated the altar between 1878 and 1886. Under an agreement between the Ottoman Empire and the German government, its relief panels were shipped to Berlin, where they became the centrepiece of the museum named after them. Turkey's culture minister demanded its return in 1998 and again in 2001.
Credit: Photo: SALT Research, no known restrictions
Story: Pergamon, above today's Bergama near İzmir, was the capital of the Attalid kings in the Hellenistic period. In the first half of the 2nd century BCE King Eumenes II built a monumental altar on its acropolis. Its frieze shows the battle between the Olympian gods and the giants, a story the Attalids used to celebrate their own victories over the Galatians. When the altar lost its function in late antiquity, its stones were reused in fortifications, and by the 19th century local residents were burning some of the marble for lime. Bergama still lives with the absence of its most famous monument.

Title: Market Gate of Miletus
Description: This Roman marble gateway once led into the southern market of Miletus. It was excavated by German archaeologists in 1903, and its fragments were transported to Berlin in 1907–1908 and reassembled as a full-size monument inside the museum.
Story: Miletus, near today's Balat in Aydın province, was one of the great cities of the Greek and Roman world. In the 2nd century CE a two-storey marble gate was built at the northern entrance to its southern market, where traders and citizens passed every day. An earthquake in the 10th or 11th century brought it down, and it lay in pieces until German archaeologists dug it up at the beginning of the 20th century.

Title: Mshatta Facade
Description: The carved stone facade of an Umayyad desert palace was given by the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II to his ally, the German Emperor Wilhelm II. A large part of it was brought to Berlin in 1903, while the plain walls of the palace remained in Jordan.
Story: Qasr Mshatta, about 30 km south of Amman, was an Umayyad winter palace probably commissioned by Caliph al-Walid II around 743–744 CE. It was never finished: after the caliph was murdered, work stopped, and an earthquake later ruined the site. The richly carved stone facade around its main entrance, with vines, rosettes and animals, is one of the earliest masterpieces of Islamic ornament. Most of the palace walls, which were left plain, still stand in Jordan; only the decorated part was taken away.

Title: Bust of Nefertiti
Description: Found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose by a German team led by Ludwig Borchardt, the bust came to Berlin through a division of finds with the French-led Egyptian Antiquities Service. Egypt has demanded its return since 1924, accusing Borchardt of concealing its value; Berlin insists on its ownership.
Story: Amarna, on the east bank of the Nile in Middle Egypt, was the short-lived capital founded by Pharaoh Akhenaten, who introduced the worship of the sun disc Aten. Nefertiti was his Great Royal Wife and possibly ruled alongside him. Around 1345 BCE the sculptor Thutmose made a painted limestone bust of her in his workshop, probably as a model for other portraits. When the city was abandoned, the workshop was buried in sand, and the bust stayed there for more than 3,000 years.

Title: Benin Bronzes
Description: Thousands of plaques and sculptures were looted from the royal palace by British forces in 1897 and sold on to museums across Europe; Berlin acquired one of the largest collections. In 2022 Germany transferred ownership of the Benin Bronzes in its public collections to Nigeria. Some have been physically returned, while others remain in Berlin on loan.
Story: The Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Edo State in southern Nigeria, was a powerful West African state with a royal court in Benin City. Guilds of brass casters and ivory carvers worked for the Oba, the king, producing plaques, heads and figures that recorded the kingdom's history, rituals and rulers and decorated the royal palace. These objects were not art for display but part of the court's memory and religious life.

Title: Ngonnso statue
Description: The statue of Ngonnso, the founding queen mother of the Nso people, was taken in 1902 during a military expedition of the German colonial army and donated to the Berlin museum. After decades of campaigning by the Nso community, the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation authorised its return in 2022; the physical handover was still pending in late 2024.
Credit: Historical photo: Felix von Luschan, public domain
Story: For the Nso people of the Bamenda grasslands in today's Cameroon, Ngonnso is the founding queen mother of their kingdom. According to oral tradition, the princess left Rifem in the 14th or 15th century after a dispute over royal succession and founded Nso. A wooden figure nearly a metre tall and covered with cowrie shells was made in her honour. She is regarded as a mother deity, a symbol of hope and peace, and rituals performed around her are meant to protect the community's survival.

Title: Luf boat
Description: This large ocean-going outrigger boat was built on Luf, a community that had been devastated by a German naval punitive expedition in 1882–1883. It was brought to Berlin in 1904. Historian Götz Aly's book Das Prachtboot (2021) sparked a public debate about whether its acquisition can be called legitimate.
Story: Luf is a small island in the Hermit Islands of today's Papua New Guinea. In 1882–1883 a German naval 'punitive expedition', launched on the initiative of the trading company Hernsheim & Co, destroyed houses and boats, killed inhabitants and looted the villages. Around 1890 the surviving men began building a large ocean-going outrigger boat, perhaps the last of its kind. In 1895 they planned to use it for the sea burial of their leader Labenan, but too few people were left to launch it, and it stayed in its boathouse.

Title: Giraffatitan skeleton
Description: The world's tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton was dug up in German East Africa by a colonial expedition that depended on local porters and labourers. Tanzanian voices have called for the fossils' return, with a request reported as early as 1987, but no return has been agreed; the museum prefers research cooperation.
Story: Tendaguru Hill in the Lindi Region of southeastern Tanzania is one of the richest dinosaur sites in the world. In 1906, while the region was part of German East Africa, local workers showed the German mining engineer Bernhard Sattler enormous bones weathering out of a path. The bones belonged to dinosaurs that lived around 150 million years ago, among them the giant sauropod now called Giraffatitan.

Title: Sphinx of Hattusa
Description: Two sphinxes from the southern gate of the Hittite capital were taken to Germany for restoration in 1917. One was sent back in 1924, but the other stayed in Berlin and was displayed in the Pergamonmuseum from 1934. After years of pressure from Turkey, it was returned in 2011 and reunited with its pair near its original site.
Story: Hattusa, near today's Boğazkale in Çorum province, was the capital of the Hittite Empire in the 2nd millennium BCE. Its southern city gate was guarded by a pair of stone sphinxes, protective figures with human heads and lion bodies. The ruins of Hattusa were rediscovered by European travellers in the 1830s, and German archaeologists began excavating there in 1906. Today the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
